analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal cigarette tax from 24 cents to $2 a pack, funding health education and aid to tobacco farmers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the cigarette tax from 24 cents to $2 per pack, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 1994 and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have sharply raised federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco, and indexed those rates to inflation. It would have cracked down on tobacco products smuggled back into the country after being labeled for export. A small share of the new revenue would have gone into a trust fund to help tobacco farmers switch to other crops and to fund health education about tobacco risks.
analysis.who_benefits: Public health: higher cigarette prices are one of the best-documented ways to cut smoking, especially among young people, so fewer people would get sick and die from tobacco. The Treasury would collect substantially more revenue. Tobacco farmers and the communities that depend on them would receive transition grants, and health education programs would receive dedicated funding.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the cigarette tax from $12 to $100 per thousand cigarettes — roughly from 24 cents to $2 per pack — with similar large increases on cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, and cigarette papers, and a new per-pound tax on roll-your-own tobacco [S2][S3].
Indexes all tobacco tax rates to inflation after 1994, so the tax does not erode over time the way the existing rates had [S3].

Creates a Tobacco Conversion and Health Education Trust Fund, funded by 3% of the new tax revenue, to help farmers convert from tobacco to other crops, retire tobacco allotments, and bring non-tobacco income to affected communities, and to fund public health education [S2][S3].

Cracks down on a smuggling loophole: it imposes penalties up to five times the evaded tax on anyone who sells or relands tobacco labeled for export back into the U.S. market, and restricts importation of previously exported products [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who are disproportionately lower-income, would bear the tax through much higher prices — the increase on a pack-a-day smoker would be roughly $640 a year. Tobacco manufacturers, tobacco farmers, wholesalers, and retailers would lose sales and face new compliance burdens, including a one-time floor-stocks tax on inventory held when the increase took effect [S3]. The treasuries of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, which receive a share of tobacco taxes, would have their share capped at the old rate [S3].

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: smokers skew lower-income, so the roughly $1.76-per-pack increase would take a much larger share of a low-income smoker's budget than a wealthier one's [S2][S3].

The transition aid is small relative to the disruption: only 3% of new revenue goes to the trust fund, with two-thirds of that for farmer conversion, while the tax increase itself is enormous — many farming communities would still face severe losses [S3].

Steep tax gaps invite smuggling and cross-border purchases; the bill's own elaborate anti-smuggling and floor-stocks provisions are an acknowledgment that a tax this large is hard to administer cleanly [S3].
Retailers would owe a one-time floor-stocks tax on tobacco inventory held on October 1, 1994, softened only by a $500 credit, a real cash burden for small shops [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong: large price increases reliably reduce smoking, especially among young people, and the smuggling and inflation loopholes the bill closes are real. But the design is blunt — the cost lands on lower-income smokers rather than on the industry's profits, and the aid for displaced farmers and towns is a thin slice of the revenue relative to the disruption a $2-per-pack tax would cause. A better-designed version would have devoted a larger share of revenue to the communities bearing the transition costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1994 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark (D-CA) introduced the bill on March 17, 1994, joined by 14 original cosponsors (13 Democrats and 1 Republican) [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that referral is the last action of any kind recorded for the bill [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, killing the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, tobacco farmers, and retailers kept the existing low tax rates, and smokers continued paying 24 cents a pack in federal tax. No constituency for the bill was powerful enough to get it a hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco makers and smokers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was almost entirely Democratic — 13 Democrats and 1 Republican out of 14 cosponsors — and the bill died in a Democratic-controlled committee without ever reaching a vote, so no party-line record exists.

industries.note: The tax would raise the federal excise on a pack of cigarettes roughly eightfold and apply similar increases across cigars, smokeless, pipe, and roll-your-own tobacco, cutting demand and profits. The industry's interest in keeping taxes low runs directly against the public health purpose of the bill.

Farmers would face sharply lower demand for their crops, but the bill directs a share of the new revenue into conversion grants, allotment retirement payments, and aid to affected towns. Their fate is tied to the same communities the bill is trying to protect.

Retailers and wholesalers would owe a one-time floor-stocks tax on inventory held when the higher rates took effect (with a $500 credit) and face new marking and import-compliance rules, while higher prices would cut sales volume.
